paragraph_content.content: Named in honour of its inventor Waloddi Weibull who introduced it for the first time in 1939 in connection with his studies on the strength of materials (see Weibull (1939)), this distribution is widely used as a model in reliability and lifetime studies (see Lawless (1982); Murthy et al. (2004); Nelson (1982)). There are many applications of the Weibull distribution in medicine, biology, agriculture, forestry and engineering sciences. In addition, the Weibull distribution has found applications as a trend curve in much applied research (see Banks (1994); Ross (1990); Seber and Wild (1989)). The reliability function
and the hazard (instantaneous failure rate) function

and hence MLE does not exist. In the literature, considerable effort has been devoted to such difficulties with the maximum likelihood approach (Cheng and Iles, 1990; Smith and Naylor, 1987). There are several other statistical methods for estimating model parameters such as the method of moments, the method of percentiles and the Bayesian method. Unfortunately, none of these methods (excluding the Bayesian one) is appropriate for small data sets (see Lawless (1982); Murthy et al. (2004); Nelson (1982)).

A very popular method for parameter estimation is the least squares (LS) method. Numerical methods for solving the nonlinear LS problem are described in Dennis and Schnabel (1996); Gill et al. (1981). Before the iterative minimization of the sum of squares it is still necessary to ask whether the least squares estimate (LSE) exists. In the case of nonlinear LS problems it is still extremely difficult to answer this question (see Bates and Watts (1988); Bjorck¨ (1996); Demidenko (2006, 2000); Hadeler et al. (2007); Jukic´ et al. (2004, 1999)).

Surprisingly, in spite of the many papers on Weibull models, we have not managed to find any paper dealing with the existence problem for a solution to a nonlinear LS problem for the three-parametric Weibull distribution.

The structure of the paper is as follows. In Section 2 we present our main result (Theorem 1) which guarantees the existence of the LSE for the three-parametric Weibull distribution. An illustrative numerical example is given in Section 3. To avoid nonnecessary technicalities at an early stage, all proofs are given in Section 4.
